transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. 

Well, what brought me in is that I keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is still seated. I'll suddenly feel like I need to go refill my coffee, or go check a handout, or I'll just walk to the back of the room. It happens even though nothing is really urgent. I just seem to have a hard time staying in my chair when I'm supposed to.
Has this difficulty staying seated been happening for a long time, or is it something more recent?

It's actually more recent. I'd say it's been noticeably harder to manage for about eight months now. That's when my youngest left for college, and the house just became a lot quieter. Ever since then, it's just been a struggle to stay put.

Besides this difficulty staying seated, have you been feeling persistently worried or anxious about things, or have you noticed a persistent low mood or loss of interest in activities you normally enjoy?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, it's an adjustment having an empty nest, but I'm not feeling down or constantly worried about things. I still enjoy teaching and my usual hobbies just as much as I always have. It's really just... well, just this trouble sitting still.
When you were a child or teenager, did you ever have trouble paying attention in school, or did teachers or parents ever say you were hyperactive or couldn't sit still in class?

Well, yes. Even as a young girl, my report cards always said I was bright, but... well, that I just could not stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother actually used to joke about it. She said I wore a path right into the floor between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten. So, yes, I definitely had trouble sitting still in class back then, too.
